content: The studies included a total of 34,584 patients and were conducted using cross-sectional and cohort designs. The diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) was evaluated for the detection of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN 2+). The following findings were observed: 1. True Positives (TP): The absolute difference in true positives was 2 fewer patients identified as having CIN 2+ when comparing the HPV test followed by visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) to cytology. This was based on 14 studies with 34,584 patients. The quality of evidence was rated as low due to serious limitations in study design and indirectness. 2. True Negatives (TN): The absolute difference in true negatives was 14 more patients correctly identified as not having CIN 2+ when using the HPV test followed by VIA compared to cytology. This was also based on 14 studies with 34,584 patients. The quality of evidence was low due to similar limitations. 3. False Positives (FP): There were 14 more false positives (patients incorrectly classified as having CIN 2+) with the HPV test followed by VIA compared to cytology. This was derived from the same 14 studies. The evidence quality was low due to imprecision and inconsistency. 4. False Negatives (FN): The absolute difference in false negatives was 14 fewer patients incorrectly classified as not having CIN 2+ when using the HPV test followed by VIA compared to cytology. Again, this was based on the same 14 studies, with low-quality evidence. 5. Mortality from Cervical Cancer: Mortality rates varied across screening strategies. For example, the HPV test followed by VIA resulted in 1,594 deaths per 1,000,000 patients, compared to 4,350 deaths in the no-screening group. Cytology followed by colposcopy resulted in 1,376 deaths per 1,000,000 patients. 6. Cervical Cancer Incidence: The incidence of cervical cancer was lower in the HPV test followed by VIA group (22,231 cases per 1,000,000 patients) compared to the no-screening group (60,750 cases per 1,000,000 patients). Cytology followed by colposcopy resulted in 19,260 cases per 1,000,000 patients. 7. CIN 2+ Recurrence: Recurrence rates of CIN 2+ were higher in the HPV test followed by VIA group (329 cases per 1,000,000 patients) compared to cytology followed by colposcopy (25 cases per 1,000,000 patients). 8. Major Bleeding: Major bleeding events were more common in patients treated with cold knife conization (CKC) compared to other treatment modalities. For example, 4,657 cases of major bleeding occurred per 1,000,000 patients treated with CKC, compared to 601 cases with loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP). 9. Premature Delivery: The risk of premature delivery was higher in patients treated with CKC (5,612 cases per 1,000,000 patients) compared to LEEP (584 cases per 1,000,000 patients). 10. Infections: Major infections were rare, with 782 cases per 1,000,000 patients treated with CKC. Minor infections were more common, with 8,867 cases per 1,000,000 patients treated with CKC. 11. Unnecessary Treatment (False Positives): The number of patients unnecessarily treated due to false positives was higher in the HPV test followed by VIA group (12,000 cases per 1,000,000 patients) compared to cytology. 12. Cancer Detected at First Screening: The number of cancers detected at the first screening was higher in the HPV test group (31,680 cases per 1,000,000 patients) compared to cytology (16,800 cases per 1,000,000 patients). Methodological Considerations: The studies were assessed for risk of bias using the QUADAS tool. Many studies only performed a single biopsy of abnormal lesions, and blinding of test results was unclear. Data for HPV testing followed by VIA and cytology followed by colposcopy were calculated based on sensitivity and specificity, as direct data were unavailable. Sensitivity and specificity estimates for HPV testing, VIA, and cytology varied despite similar cut-off values, leading to inconsistency in results. Wide confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity, specificity, and other outcomes may lead to different clinical decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. Sensitivity and Specificity: HPV testing had a pooled sensitivity of 94% (95% CI: 89–97%) and specificity of 90% (95% CI: 86–93%). VIA had a pooled sensitivity of 69% (95% CI: 54–81%) and specificity of 87% (95% CI: 79–92%). Cytology (ASCUS) had a pooled sensitivity of 70% (95% CI: 57–81%) and specificity of 95% (95% CI: 92–97%). Quality of Evidence: The overall quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low due to limitations in study design, indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision. This lack of confidence in the effect estimates stems from the low quality of evidence for treatment effects and natural progression data. Assumptions: Mortality from cervical cancer was assumed to be zero in true negatives (TN) and false positives (FP). The incidence of cervical cancer was based on age-standardized rates from Eastern Africa, with assumptions about the natural persistence and regression of CIN 2+. Major bleeding, premature delivery, and infection risks were estimated based on pooled proportions from observational studies without independent controls. These findings highlight the need for careful consideration of the trade-offs between sensitivity, specificity, and the potential harms of screening and treatment strategies for cervical cancer.
